name: Safety glasses
summary: Impact-rated glasses with side protection that stop flying chips and fragments; they don't seal against splashes or fine dust.
uses: Flying chips, wire ends and glass when cutting, prying, grinding or smashing; Z87+ is the high-impact grade (HexArmor Z87)
Under a face shield or welding helmet for impact and chemical work: the glasses are the eye protection, the shield adds to it (OSHA shipyard eTool; OSHA 3151)
UV light: a U mark means a UV tint. Many polycarbonate lenses absorb UV, but a coloured lens can give none, so tint tells you nothing (NIOSH eyewear bulletin; CCOHS eye protectors)
Not for splashes or fine dust: liquid gets past open frames, so wear goggles with indirect vents or none (NC State eye PPE; CDC eye protection)
Not for welding, torch work or lasers unless the lens carries a shade number or a laser rating (OSHA 1910.133; OSHA 3151)
Choose plastic frames around live wiring: metal frames shouldn't be used where there are electrical hazards (OSHA shipyard eTool)
identify: Real safety glasses are marked on both the frame and the lens (NIOSH eyewear bulletin). US marks: Z87 means the basic impact test; Z87+ means it also passed the high-velocity and high-mass impact tests (HexArmor Z87); prescription safety frames say Z87-2 or Z87-2+. Other lens marks: U for a UV tint and R for an infrared tint (NIOSH eyewear bulletin); D3 droplets and splash, D4 dust, D5 fine dust (HexArmor Z87). Glasses with side protection still give less splash protection than goggles (CDC eye protection). Canada: CSA Z94.3 class 1 spectacles (1A impact, 1B impact plus a radiation filter); a certifier's mark such as CSA or SEI beside Z94.3 means third-party tested, while 'Z94.3' alone is the maker's own claim (HexArmor CSA). Europe: EN 166 with a strength letter: S (increased robustness), F (45 m/s), B (120 m/s) or A (190 m/s); EN ISO 16321 is replacing it (uvex EN 166). Not safety glasses: everyday glasses marked ANSI Z80 (an optics standard), and sports eyewear to ASTM F803 (NIOSH eyewear bulletin). Glass lenses don't meet CSA impact rules, and tint is no guide to UV protection (CCOHS eye protectors).
test: Read the marks first: no Z87, Z94.3 or EN 166 on frame and lens means unrated. Hold each lens up to the light and reject any that is pitted, cracked or deeply scratched: damaged lenses break more easily on impact (NC State eye PPE; CCOHS eye protectors). Bent frames, loose lenses and broken side shields go too. Fit: they should cover from eyebrow to cheekbone and from the nose to the side of the face, and sit close (CCOHS eye protectors); OSHA wants side protection wherever bits can fly (OSHA 1910.133). Over prescription glasses, the safety pair must not shift your own lenses (OSHA 1910.133). Clean with mild soap and water and air-dry; silicone cleaners spoil anti-fog coatings, and after contact with dangerous chemicals uvex says to throw them away (uvex FAQ). Note the date: uvex gives its glasses six years' shelf life in the box if kept dry, dark and under 40 °C, and at most two years of use (uvex FAQ).

decay.note: Estimate from one maker: uvex gives boxed glasses 6 years from manufacture if dry, dark, under 40 °C and below 70% humidity, and at most 2 years of use (uvex FAQ). Scratched or pitted lenses must go (CCOHS eye protectors).

improvise: Best stand-ins: impact-rated goggles, or a full-face respirator, whose lens must meet the same impact rules (CCOHS eye protectors). A face shield alone won't give adequate protection against impact (OSHA 3151); it only adds to goggles or safety spectacles worn under it (OSHA 3151; OSHA shipyard eTool). Everyday prescription glasses are not protection: the lenses may shatter and there are no side shields (SAIF; OSHA 3151); wear goggles that fit over them, or safety glasses made to fit over them or with your prescription built in (OSHA 1910.133; OSHA 3151). Ordinary sunglasses are generally not eye protection: only eyewear marked Z87 counts (UF/IFAS sunglasses). Sports goggles to ASTM F803 are not allowed as a substitute for work eyewear (NIOSH eyewear bulletin). Contact lenses are not enough on their own: wearers still need eye protection (CDC eye protection; OSHA 3151). Avoid metal frames near live wiring (OSHA shipyard eTool). Better still, change the job: smash or cut inside a box or under a heavy cloth, stand aside from anything springy, and keep other people back.
